kurals.tamil:
வினைத்திட்பம் என்பது ஒருவன் மனத்திட்பம்
மற்றைய எல்லாம் பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaiththitpam enpadhu oruvan manaththitpam
Matraiya ellaam piRa.
kurals.meaning: What is called firmness in action is really a person’s firmness of mind; every other kind of strength is something else and does not deserve that name.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two kids building a tall block tower. Both have the same blocks, but one gives up when it wobbles and the other keeps going. The blocks are not what made the difference. The strong part was inside the kid who kept going. That inside strength is what gets things done.
kurals.university: The chapter title vinai-t-tiṭpam pairs vinai (undertaking, action) with tiṭpam (solidity, firmness), and the opening couplet at once relocates that firmness from the deed to the doer: vinai-t-tiṭpam is maṉa-t-tiṭpam, firmness of mind. Parimelazhagar glosses maṟṟaiya ellām (all the others) as the external supports a minister or king might count on, such as army, fortifications, wealth and allies, and says these are piṟa, other things, not what is meant by the word. The chapter follows directly on vinai-t-tūymai (ch. 66, purity of means), so the Amaichiyal sequence runs: choose clean means, then carry them through with an unshaken mind. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading closely (Pappaiah: the resolve not to abandon a task midway), while Kalaignar turns it conditionally: whatever else one has, without firmness of mind there is no firmness in action. The text is identical in ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are on this path are resolute in purpose, and their aim is one. O beloved child of the Kurus, the intelligence of those who are irresolute is many-branched.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna contrasts the single-pointed, resolute intellect (vyavasāyātmikā buddhi) with the scattered mind of the irresolute.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts locate the power to act in a firmly resolved mind rather than in outward means.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.41 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match on resolute mind; the Gita’s context is spiritual discipline rather than statecraft.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a divided, wavering mind makes a person unreliable in everything he does.
christianity.tie_back: The negative form of the Kural’s claim: an unsteady mind produces unsteady action.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match stated negatively; James is speaking of faith in prayer, not of executing tasks.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, those who have said, "Our Lord is Allah" and then remained on a right course - the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve...”
islam.explanation: The verse praises istiqāma, standing firm on a course once it has been professed, and promises divine support to those who do.
islam.tie_back: Steadfastness after the decision, not the decision alone, is what counts, as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the ideal of inner steadfastness, but applies it to faith rather than to worldly undertakings.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They are not afraid of evil tidings; their heart is firm, they trust in GOD.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm describes the righteous person whose firm heart keeps him unshaken by bad news.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Their heart is firm’ is almost a translation of maṉa-t-tiṭpam, the firmness of mind the Kural makes central.
judaism.source: Psalms 112:7 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close verbal match on a firm heart; the psalm grounds it in trust in God rather than in action.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens by teaching that every deed and its result flows from the state of the mind behind it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the mind, not outward factors, the true source of what an action becomes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the primacy of mind over outward means; the Buddhist verse concerns moral purity rather than firmness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Heart, be still, you had worse than this to bear on the day when the terrible Cyclops ate your brave companions...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised in his own house, Odysseus holds his anger in check by speaking to his heart, so that his plan against the suitors is not wrecked by impulse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus’s success comes from mastering his own mind, the firmness the Kural calls the real power in action.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A vivid dramatization of inner firmness serving a plan; it is narrative, not a stated maxim.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus divides the world into what belongs to our own mind and will, and externals such as body, property and office, which ‘belong to others’.
philosophy.tie_back: His split mirrors the Kural’s: the mind’s firmness is one’s own, and ‘all the others are other’.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel between inner and external goods, though Epictetus aims at tranquillity rather than accomplishment.

kurals.tamil:
ஊறொரால் உற்றபின் ஒல்காமை இவ்விரண்டின்
ஆறென்பர் ஆய்ந்தவர் கோள்.
kurals.transliteration:
OoRoraal utrapin olkaamai ivviraNdin
AaRenpar aaindhavar koaL.
kurals.meaning: Those who have studied the matter say that firmness in action follows two rules: avoid harm before it comes, and do not give way when it has come anyway.
kurals.elementary: Before riding your bike, you check the tyres and wear a helmet so you don’t get hurt. But if you still fall, you don’t quit biking forever; you get up and keep riding. Being careful first, and being brave after, are the two secrets of finishing things.
kurals.university: The couplet sets out a two-part rule: ūṟu orāl, keeping clear of harm (ūṟu, injury or obstacle; orāl, avoidance), and uṟṟa piṉ olkāmai, not flagging (olku, to shrink or slacken) once harm has struck. Parimelazhagar reads the first clause as not undertaking an act likely to come to grief, and the ‘āyntavar’ (those who have investigated) as the authors of the political treatises (nīti nūl), so that the couplet cites a consensus of statecraft; Solomon Pappaiah follows him. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar instead read the first clause as removing an obstacle before it arrives, which puts more weight on foresight than on choice of task. Either way, firmness is shown to include prudence, not mere stubbornness, which links this chapter back to terintu ceyal vakai (ch. 47). The three web texts agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sthita-prajña, the person whose mind stays level when suffering arrives.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s second rule, not shrinking once harm has come.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.56 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘unshaken after harm’ half only; the Gita says nothing here about avoiding harm beforehand.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers to count the cost of an undertaking beforehand, lest they begin and be mocked for failing to finish.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s first rule: foresee the trouble before it comes, so the work can be carried through.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match for the foresight half; Luke’s point is the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient,”
islam.explanation: The Quran says trials will come regardless and praises ṣabr, patient steadfastness, in meeting them.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s second rule, it assumes setbacks will come and makes not buckling under them the virtue.
islam._accuracy_note: Covers endurance after harm; the prevention half has no direct counterpart here.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Seven times a righteous person falls and gets up, While the wicked are tripped by one misfortune.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the righteous, who rise again after repeated falls, with the wicked, whom one blow undoes; elsewhere (22:3) it praises the shrewd person who sees trouble coming and takes cover.
judaism.tie_back: Taken together, the two proverbs give both halves of the Kural’s rule, foresight and refusing to stay down.
judaism.source: Proverbs 24:16 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria); cf. Proverbs 22:3
judaism._accuracy_note: Two verses of the same book together cover both halves of the Kural’s rule.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sabbāsava Sutta the Buddha lists different ways of abandoning the mental effluents, among them some to be abandoned by avoiding (keeping away from a wild elephant, a thorny place, bad company) and some to be abandoned by enduring (bearing cold, heat, hunger and harsh words).
buddhism.explanation: The discourse treats avoiding and enduring as two distinct, complementary skills in dealing with harm.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural’s pair: ūṟu orāl (avoid) and olkāmai (endure without giving way).
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking structural match of avoiding plus enduring, applied to spiritual practice rather than worldly action.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Forewarned by Circe, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so the Sirens cannot lure the ship to ruin; soon afterwards, when Scylla seizes six of his men, he grieves but sails on.
greek_mythology.explanation: The episode shows both preventing a known danger before it strikes and pressing on after an unavoidable loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus follows the Kural’s two rules in a single voyage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Narrative illustration, not a stated principle; the two-part pattern fits well.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Writing after a fire destroyed the city of Lugdunum (Lyon) overnight, Seneca urges Lucilius to rehearse possible misfortunes in advance, so that nothing strikes the mind as unexpected and it is not crushed when disaster comes.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic praemeditatio malorum prepares the mind beforehand so that it stays firm afterwards.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like the Kural, joins foresight before harm with steadiness after it.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 91 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Stoic foresight prepares the mind, whereas the Kural’s first rule avoids the harm itself.

kurals.tamil:
கடைக்கொட்கச் செய்தக்க தாண்மை இடைக்கொட்கின்
எற்றா விழுமந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadaikkotkach seydhakka thaaNmai idaikkotkin
Etraa vizhumanh tharum.
kurals.meaning: True capability lies in carrying out a task so that it becomes known only when it is finished; if it leaks out midway, it brings trouble that cannot be undone.
kurals.elementary: If you are making a surprise birthday card for your mom and you show it to her half-done, the surprise is ruined and you can’t get it back. It is better to work quietly and show it when it’s finished. Some plans work best when they are kept secret until they are done.
kurals.university: The key verb is koṭku, to become manifest: kaṭai-k-koṭka, so that it appears at the end, versus iṭai-k-koṭkiṉ, if it appears in the middle. Āṇmai is literally ‘manliness’ but here means competence or mastery in execution (Solomon Pappaiah renders it āḷumai, capability), and eṟṟā vizhumam is sorrow that cannot be removed. Parimelazhagar explains that a plan disclosed before completion lets enemies obstruct it, so secrecy is part of firmness; Kalaignar makes the point explicitly, calling concealment till completion the very ‘firmness of execution’. This couplet echoes the Arthashastra tradition on the secrecy of counsel (mantra-rakṣā) and anticipates the chapter on the conduct of affairs (ch. 68). Some readers print the first line with sandhi, ceytakkatāṇmai; the three sources consulted agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya’s chapter on the business of council insists that deliberation be held in secret and that no outsider learn of a plan before it is carried out, since disclosure ruins undertakings and brings disaster to the king.
hinduism.explanation: The Arthashastra makes guarding the secrecy of counsel (mantra) a basic rule of statecraft.
hinduism.tie_back: It gives the political reasoning behind the Kural: a plan revealed midway is exposed to its enemies.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match from the same Indian polity tradition that Parimelazhagar draws on; paraphrased, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus declines to go publicly to the feast, saying his time has not yet come, then goes quietly and reveals himself only midway through the festival.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows a purpose that is kept hidden until the right moment for it to be revealed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Next-best match: secrecy about timing, but not a general maxim about concealing plans until completion.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers or they will contrive against you a plan...”
islam.explanation: Jacob tells young Joseph to keep his dream of future greatness to himself, since disclosing it early will stir his brothers’ envy and plotting.
islam.tie_back: The same logic as the Kural: revealing a destiny or plan before it is fulfilled invites obstruction.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear parallel on premature disclosure inviting harm; concerns a dream rather than an undertaking.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I got up at night, I and a few men with me, and telling no one what my God had put into my mind to do for Jerusalem...”
judaism.explanation: Nehemiah surveys Jerusalem’s broken walls by night and tells no one his plan (2:16 adds that even the officials knew nothing) until he is ready to begin the rebuilding.
judaism.tie_back: A textbook case of the Kural’s counsel: keep the work hidden until it can go forward, since enemies will try to stop it.
judaism.source: Nehemiah 2:12, 2:16 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match, including the opposition that follows once the plan becomes public.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka the wise Mahosadha, the Bodhisatta, has a great tunnel dug in secret and lets its existence be known only when it is complete and his king must be rescued.
buddhism.explanation: The Jātaka praises the sage’s concealed preparation, which succeeds because rivals do not learn of it in time.
buddhism.tie_back: The tunnel is revealed only at the end, as the Kural advises.
buddhism.source: Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka (No. 546), summary in Malalasekera’s Dictionary of Pali Proper Names
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit, though secrecy is not a doctrinal teaching in Buddhism; details are from a secondary summary.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus stays disguised as a beggar in his own palace and reveals himself only after he has strung the great bow and his vengeance on the suitors has begun.
greek_mythology.explanation: His return succeeds because his identity and plan stay hidden until the decisive moment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His concealment until the deed is under way is the Kural’s kaṭai-k-koṭka in action.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close fit: premature disclosure would have been fatal, just as the Kural warns.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night, and when you move, fall like a thunderbolt.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu advises that intentions be kept wholly hidden until the moment of action.
philosophy.tie_back: The same strategic rule as the Kural: hide the plan, and let it be seen only in its result.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War VII.19 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-direct match from a comparable statecraft text.

kurals.tamil:
சொல்லுதல் யார்க்கும் எளிய அரியவாம்
சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Solludhal yaarkkum eLiya ariyavaam
Solliya vaNNam seyal.
kurals.meaning: Anyone can say how a thing should be done; what is hard is doing it exactly as it was said.
kurals.elementary: It is easy to say, “I will clean my whole room today!” It is much harder to actually pick up every sock and toy. Anyone can make a promise; the strong person is the one who does what they said.
kurals.university: The couplet balances eḷiya (easy) against ariya (hard, rare), and solludal (saying) against solliya vaṇṇam seyal (acting in the manner that was said). Parimelazhagar takes solludal as stating how a task ought to be carried out, the counsel a minister gives, so the couplet sets planning and advice against execution; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan follow him, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar widen it to any promise or declaration. The plural eḷiya / ariya (literally ‘easy things’, ‘hard things’) is idiomatic and is normally rendered in the singular. In the chapter’s argument the couplet explains why firmness of mind is needed at all: plans are cheap, and only a firm mind turns word into deed. All three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The mind is restless, turbulent, obstinate and very strong, O Kṛṣṇa, and to subdue it, I think, is more difficult than controlling the wind.”
hinduism.explanation: After hearing Krishna’s teaching on meditation, Arjuna objects that it is easily described but extremely hard to put into practice.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna voices the Kural’s point: stating the method is easy, carrying it out is hard.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.34 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Captures the gap between teaching and practice, but frames it as mastering the mind rather than keeping one’s word.

christianity.quote_or_event: “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus criticises teachers whose instructions are sound but who do not practise them themselves.
christianity.tie_back: ‘They say, and do not’ is the failing the Kural has in view.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close match on the gap between words and deeds.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.”
islam.explanation: The Quran rebukes believers who announce intentions or commitments and then fail to act on them.
islam.tie_back: It condemns the very gap between saying and doing that the Kural calls the hard part.
islam._accuracy_note: Near-direct match; the Quran adds strong moral censure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much...”
judaism.explanation: Shammai tells students to promise little and accomplish much, putting deeds ahead of words.
judaism.tie_back: A practical answer to the Kural’s observation that talk is easy and deeds are hard.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:15 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match, phrased as advice rather than observation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: Fine words not put into practice are compared to a flower that looks lovely but has no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts value the doing over the saying.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on words without deeds being empty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the Boasting Traveler, a man brags of a giant leap he made at Rhodes and offers witnesses; a bystander tells him to suppose this is Rhodes and leap for them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable punctures boasting by demanding the deed itself, here and now.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The bystander’s challenge makes the Kural’s point: claiming is easy, doing is the test.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Boasting Traveler (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Greek fable rather than myth proper, but a very close thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never call yourself a philosopher, nor talk a great deal among the unlearned about theorems, but act conformably to them.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells his students to show their philosophy by how they live, not by talking about it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats acting in line with one’s words as the real, and harder, achievement.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on practice over talk.

kurals.tamil:
வீறெய்தி மாண்டார் வினைத்திட்பம் வேந்தன்கண்
ஊறெய்தி உள்ளப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
VeeReydhi maaNdaar vinaiththitpam vaendhankaN
OoReydhi uLLap padum.
kurals.meaning: The firmness in action of those who have risen to distinction reaches the king himself, and so it comes to be held in high regard by all.
kurals.elementary: When a student works hard and finishes a great project, the teacher notices, then the principal hears about it, and soon the whole school knows. Steady, finished work travels up to the people in charge, and everyone respects it.
kurals.university: Vīṟu is distinction or excellence and māṇṭār those who are great or eminent; the verb māḷ can also mean ‘to die’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss on ytamizh.com reads the phrase as ‘those who died valiantly’, but the mainstream commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesikan) take māṇṭār as ‘the eminent’. Parimelazhagar specifies that their eminence comes from excellence of counsel (eṇṇam), and that their firmness in execution, by ‘reaching’ the king (vēntaṉkaṇ ūṟu eyti, where ūṟu means contact or effect, not harm as in 662), is then esteemed by everyone (uḷḷappaṭum). The couplet thus explains how a minister’s firmness is rewarded: it becomes visible through the ruler’s regard. Pope’s ‘With king acceptance finds and fame through all the state’ follows the same reading. The three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna notes that the deeds of eminent people become the standard everyone else follows.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the firm action of the great becomes widely known and honoured.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the public influence of great men’s actions; lacks the Kural’s link to royal recognition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things...”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the talents, the servant who carried his charge through faithfully is praised and promoted by his master.
christianity.tie_back: Diligent execution reaches the lord’s notice and wins honour, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good fit on recognition of faithful work by the master; parable frame is eschatological.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the king said, "Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself." And when he spoke to him, he said, "Indeed, you are today established [in position] and trusted."”
islam.explanation: Having seen Joseph’s wisdom and integrity, the king of Egypt takes him into his own service and gives him high standing.
islam.tie_back: Joseph’s proven worth ‘reaches the king’ and brings him esteem, as the Kural describes.
islam._accuracy_note: Close narrative match of a capable minister recognised by a ruler.

judaism.quote_or_event: “See a man skilled at his work— He shall attend upon kings; He shall not attend upon the lowly.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that someone who excels at his work will end up serving before kings.
judaism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact claim: excellence in action reaches the king.
judaism.source: Proverbs 22:29 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the reputation of an energetic, disciplined person keeps growing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say sustained, disciplined action brings growing renown.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches growing esteem from energetic conduct; no reference to a king.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Then the king knew that he must be the valiant offspring of a god, so he kept him in Lycia, gave him his daughter in marriage, and made him of equal honour in the kingdom with himself...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Sent by the Lycian king on deadly tasks, Bellerophon completes each one (the Chimaera, the Solymi, the Amazons, an ambush), and the king finally honours him instead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Bellerophon’s firmness in carrying out every task reaches the king and wins him the highest honour.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; the king’s motive was originally hostile, which the Kural does not envisage.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...honour is the prize of virtue, and it is to the good that it is rendered.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that honour is the proper reward that follows real excellence.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise has esteem follow proven excellence in action.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: General principle of honour following excellence; not specific to execution or royal notice.

kurals.tamil:
எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப எண்ணியார்
திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
ENNiya eNNiyaangu eydhupa eNNiyaar
ThiNNiyar aagap peRin.
kurals.meaning: If those who plan are firm in carrying out their plans, they will attain what they aimed at, and in just the way they aimed at it.
kurals.elementary: If you decide to learn to ride a bike and you keep practising every day, even after wobbling, you will ride just the way you imagined. Wishing is the start; sticking with it is what makes the wish come true.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on eṇṇu (to think, plan) four times: eṇṇiya (what was planned), eṇṇiyāṅku (as it was planned), eṇṇiyār (those who planned), set against tiṇṇiyar (the firm), which chimes with tiṭpam in the chapter title. Parimelazhagar reads it as a promise conditional on firmness in execution: planners who are also firm doers obtain both the object and the manner they intended; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print eytu (எய்து), but the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org has eytupa (எய்துப, ‘they will attain’, future plural), and thirukkural.net’s own musical setting of the couplet by P. A. Muthukrishnan also quotes எய்துப; that reading, which the metre and grammar need, is adopted here. The couplet is one of the most often quoted in the Porul section, as a maxim that resolve turns intention into result.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Bhagīratha undertakes long austerities to bring the celestial Gaṅgā down to earth for his ancestors, persisting through each obstacle until Śiva agrees to bear her fall and the river reaches its goal.
hinduism.explanation: His persistence is so proverbial that ‘Bhagīratha prayatna’ (Bhagiratha’s effort) is a common Indian phrase for relentless, successful effort.
hinduism.tie_back: Bhagīratha attains exactly what he set out to do because he stays firm, as the Kural promises.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Illustrative narrative of resolve achieving its aim; paraphrased from the Purana.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea; and shall not doubt in his heart, but shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass; he shall have whatsoever he saith.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that an undivided, undoubting heart obtains what it asks for.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties getting what one intends to an unwavering inner firmness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Structural match (firmness leads to attainment), but Mark speaks of faith in God, not firmness in execution.

islam.quote_or_event: “And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that a person gains only what he has actively striven for.
islam.tie_back: Both texts tie attainment to sustained effort toward the intended end.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the link between striving and attaining; its main context is accountability before God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...along the path a person wishes to proceed, one leads and assists him.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar draws from Torah, Prophets and Writings the principle that a person is helped along whatever path he firmly chooses.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a settled intention is carried to fulfilment along the course it has chosen.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Makkot 10b (William Davidson Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel on intention shaping outcome; the Talmud credits divine guidance rather than human firmness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Gladly would I let the flesh & blood in my body dry up, leaving just the skin, tendons, & bones, but if I have not attained what can be reached through human firmness, human persistence, human striving, there will be no relaxing my persistence.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) of a committed disciple, who will not relax effort until the goal is reached, and says such a disciple can expect the fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Human firmness’ leading to attainment is the Kural’s tiṇṇiyar reaching what they planned.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 70, Kitagiri Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match, including the explicit word ‘firmness’ and the promised result.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Nevertheless, I want to get home, and can think of nothing else. If some god wrecks me when I am on the sea, I will bear it and make the best of it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Offered immortality by Calypso, Odysseus holds to his single aim of returning home, and in the end he gets there.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His fixed intention, held firmly through every setback, reaches its goal just as he meant it to.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative parallel on single-minded resolve bringing its aim to pass.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that our plans miscarry because they have no fixed aim, and that when a man does not know which harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, a firmly fixed purpose is the precondition for any course of action to succeed.
philosophy.tie_back: He matches the Kural’s point that attainment follows a settled, firmly held intention.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 71 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; stresses a clear aim more than firmness in carrying it out.

kurals.tamil:
உருவுகண்டு எள்ளாமை வேண்டும் உருள்பெருந்தேர்க்கு
அச்சாணி அன்னார் உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
UruvukaNdu eLLaamai vaeNdum uruLperundhaerkku
AchchaaNi annaar udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: No one should be scorned for their small size or plain looks, for the world has people who are like the little linchpin that holds the wheel of a great rolling chariot.
kurals.elementary: A giant temple chariot has huge wheels, but a tiny metal pin keeps each wheel from falling off. Without that little pin, the whole chariot stops! Some people are small or quiet, but they hold everything together, so never laugh at someone for being small.
kurals.university: Uru (form, size, appearance) and eḷḷāmai (not despising) open the couplet, and its image is the accāṇi, the small pin driven through the end of the axle (accu) that keeps the wheel of a great rolling temple chariot (uruḷ perun tēr) in place. Parimelazhagar, and Solomon Pappaiah after him, apply it within the chapter’s theme: men of firm mind may be small in body yet great in achievement, so they must not be judged by appearance; Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar give it the wider moral that no one should be belittled for their size. The couplet reverses the usual link between bulk and strength, placing strength once again in firmness rather than outward form, as in 661. The three sources agree on the text; in sandhi form the lines read uruvukaṇ ṭeḷḷāmai vēṇṭu muruḷperuntērk / kaccāṇi yaṉṉā ruṭaittu.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Viṣṇu comes to King Bali’s sacrifice as Vāmana, a dwarf brahmin boy, and asks for just three steps of land; granted it, he grows to cosmic size and covers the earth and heavens in two strides.
hinduism.explanation: The Vāmana avatāra is India’s classic warning that small size can hide immeasurable power.
hinduism.tie_back: Bali’s court, seeing only a dwarf, learns what the Kural teaches: never judge strength by size.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; a divine narrative rather than a maxim about human worth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.”
christianity.explanation: James points out that a huge ship is steered by a tiny rudder, to show how a small thing can control a great one.
christianity.tie_back: The helm and the linchpin make the same point: a small part can govern a great vessel.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-identical image; James applies it to the tongue rather than to underrated people.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that worth is measured by inner disposition and deeds, not by outward appearance or means.
islam.tie_back: Both texts forbid judging people by their outward form.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on not judging by appearance; lacks the linchpin image of the small but indispensable.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But GOD said to Samuel, “Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature, for I have rejected him. For [GOD sees] not as humans see; humans see only what is visible, but GOD sees into the heart.””
judaism.explanation: Sent to anoint a king, Samuel is warned not to be impressed by Eliab’s height; the chosen one is the youngest, the overlooked shepherd David.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Pay no attention to his appearance or his stature’ is almost the Kural’s uruvu kaṇṭu eḷḷāmai.
judaism.source: 1 Samuel 16:7 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close match, reinforced by the David narrative that follows.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Venerable Bhaddiya the Dwarf (Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya), whose small and unattractive body drew mockery, is taken by Sāriputta for a mere learner; the Buddha declares that Bhaddiya has already cut the cycle and reached freedom.
buddhism.explanation: The Udāna records the Buddha correcting a senior disciple who misjudged a small monk’s attainment.
buddhism.tie_back: The dwarf-monk is the Kural’s linchpin: small in form, complete in achievement.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match; the mockery of his looks comes from the commentarial tradition, the misjudgment from the sutta itself.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...now you know that it is possible for even a Mouse to confer benefits on a Lion.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The lion laughs at a mouse’s promise to repay him, but when the lion is caught in hunters’ ropes, the mouse gnaws him free.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The despised small creature proves indispensable, just as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, The Lion and the Mouse (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Classic Greek fable with near-identical moral; fable rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I say, that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus, which are set up in the statuaries’ shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths; and they are made to open in the middle, and have images of gods inside them.”
philosophy.explanation: Alcibiades compares Socrates, notoriously ugly, to cheap satyr figurines that open to reveal golden images of gods inside.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is the philosopher’s linchpin: unimpressive outside, indispensable within.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on the gap between appearance and worth.

kurals.tamil:
கலங்காது கண்ட வினைக்கண் துளங்காது
தூக்கங் கடிந்து செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kalangaadhu kaNda vinaikkaN thuLangaadhu
ThookkanG kadindhu seyal.
kurals.meaning: Once a course of action has been settled with a clear mind, carry it out without wavering and without delay.
kurals.elementary: When you and your friends decide to build a treehouse, first think carefully. But once you’ve decided, don’t keep changing your mind or saying “maybe tomorrow.” Grab the hammer and start building!
kurals.university: The couplet moves in three steps: kalaṅkātu kaṇṭa vinai, an undertaking seen or decided without confusion (kalaṅku, to be muddied or agitated); tuḷaṅkātu, without wavering (tuḷaṅku, to tremble or sway); and tūkkam kaṭintu, having cast off tūkkam. Parimelazhagar takes tūkkam here as procrastination or delay (nīṭṭittal), not literal sleep, and the modern commentators follow him (Pappaiah: ‘without faltering and without delay’); Pope’s ‘mind unslumbering’ keeps the literal sense. The logic is that deliberation belongs before the decision, and firmness after it, which echoes the rule about deliberating and then acting in terintu ceyal vakai (ch. 47). The sandhi text reads viṉaikkaṭ ṭuḷaṅkātu, the same words written with the sandhi applied.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arjuna said: My dear Kṛṣṇa, O infallible one, my illusion is now gone. I have regained my memory by Your mercy. I am now firm and free from doubt and am prepared to act according to Your instructions.”
hinduism.explanation: After long deliberation, Arjuna’s confusion clears and he declares himself firm and ready to act.
hinduism.tie_back: Clear decision (kalaṅkātu kaṇṭa) followed by unwavering action is exactly the Kural’s sequence.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.73 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structural match: doubt removed, then firm action.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to hold firm and keep working, confident their work is not wasted.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Stedfast, unmoveable’ answers to the Kural’s tuḷaṅkātu, never swaying once the work is begun.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on unwavering persistence; does not address delay.

islam.quote_or_event: “...and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, then rely upon Allah. Indeed, Allah loves those who rely [upon Him].”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to take counsel, and then, once a decision is made, to act on it with trust instead of hesitating.
islam.tie_back: Consultation, then firm and prompt action, is the Kural’s own sequence.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; adds reliance on God (tawakkul).

judaism.quote_or_event: “He [also] used to say: If I am not for myself, who is for me? But if I am for my own self [only], what am I? And if not now, when?”
judaism.explanation: Hillel’s last question rejects putting off what ought to be done.
judaism.tie_back: ‘If not now, when?’ is the Kural’s tūkkam kaṭintu, casting off delay.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:14 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘without delay’ element; says nothing about prior clear deliberation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hasten to do good; restrain your mind from evil. He who is slow in doing good, his mind delights in evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that delay in doing good leaves room for the mind to drift to harm.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts treat delay as the enemy of a good act already decided on.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on promptness; moral rather than practical context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Gordium, Alexander is shown the famous knot said to promise rule of Asia to whoever undoes it; according to the popular version, he does not hesitate but cuts it through with his sword.
greek_mythology.explanation: The ‘Gordian knot’ has become the byword for decisive action that refuses to be stalled.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alexander acts without wavering or delay once his course is set, as the Kural urges.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 18 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Legend rather than myth; Plutarch also reports a less dramatic version (pulling out the pole-pin), so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present- I am rising to the work of a human being.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues himself out of lingering in bed by recalling that he exists for action.
philosophy.tie_back: This is tūkkam kaṭintu in its literal and figurative sense: shake off sloth and do the work.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on overcoming sloth; lacks the element of prior clear decision.

kurals.tamil:
துன்பம் உறவரினும் செய்க துணிவாற்றி
இன்பம் பயக்கும் வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunpam uRavarinum seyka thuNivaatri
Inpam payakkum vinai.
kurals.meaning: Even if much hardship comes along the way, carry on boldly with the work that will bring joy in the end.
kurals.elementary: Learning to swim can be scary: water gets in your nose and your arms get tired. But if you keep going, one day you’ll zoom across the pool and love it. Some good things feel hard at first and happy at the end, so keep being brave.
kurals.university: The couplet sets tuṉpam (suffering) against iṉpam (joy), with the concessive uṟa variṉum, ‘even if it comes in abundance’ (uṟa, intensely), and the command ceyka tuṇivu āṟṟi, ‘act, sustaining courage’. Parimelazhagar explains that the suffering belongs to the beginning or the course of the undertaking while the joy is its fruit at the end, so a firm mind must not judge a task by its first taste; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah add ‘in the end’ (muṭivil) to make this explicit. Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, defining a joy-bringing act as one carried through despite suffering. The couplet sets up the chapter’s conclusion in 670. The three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines sāttvika happiness as the kind that is bitter at first and sweet in the end.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost a gloss on the Kural: accept early pain for the joy the deed will yield.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.37 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical structure of pain first, joy after.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews admits that discipline is painful while it lasts but says it later bears good fruit.
christianity.tie_back: The same pattern as the Kural, grievous now and fruitful afterward.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural match; concerns God’s discipline rather than a chosen undertaking.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease. Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.”
islam.explanation: Repeated for emphasis, the verse assures that relief comes with and after hardship.
islam.tie_back: It gives the same encouragement as the Kural, to persist through tuṉpam toward iṉpam.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the hardship-to-ease arc; not framed as a command to act.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They who sow in tears shall reap with songs of joy.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm pictures labour done in sorrow that yields a joyful harvest.
judaism.tie_back: Sowing in tears and reaping in joy is the Kural’s arc from tuṉpam to iṉpam.
judaism.source: Psalms 126:5 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match, including the image of work whose fruit comes later.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the taking on of a practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasure in the future.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha classifies undertakings by their present and future results and commends the path that is hard now but brings happiness later.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the kind of act the Kural tells us to press on with.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 45, Culadhammasamadana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on the painful-now, pleasant-later type of undertaking.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first; but when a man has reached the top, then is she easy to reach...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod pictures the path to excellence as steep and rough at first but easy once the summit is reached.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts tell us to accept the early hardship for the good at the end.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 289-292 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on hardship first, reward after; Hesiod’s frame is the pursuit of virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Diogenes Laertius reports Aristotle’s saying that the roots of education are bitter but its fruit is sweet.
philosophy.explanation: The maxim, attributed to Aristotle, holds that the hard early stages of learning are repaid by its rewards.
philosophy.tie_back: Bitter root and sweet fruit is the Kural’s suffering-then-joy in another image.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.18 (trans. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a later anecdotal source; attribution to Aristotle is traditional rather than certain.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்திட்பம் எய்தியக் கண்ணும் வினைத்திட்பம்
வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththitpam eydhiyak kaNNum vinaiththitpam
VaeNdaarai vaeNdaadhu ulagu.
kurals.meaning: Whatever other strengths they may have, the world does not value those who do not value firmness in action.
kurals.elementary: A kid might be the fastest runner, the best drawer and the funniest in class, but if they never finish their part of the group project, nobody wants them on the team. Finishing what you start matters more than all the other talents.
kurals.university: The final couplet closes the chapter in a ring: eṉai-t-tiṭpam (firmness of whatever kind) echoes vinai-t-tiṭpam, and the line turns on the repeated vēṇṭu (to want, to value): vēṇṭārai vēṇṭātu, ‘does not want those who do not want’ firmness of action. Parimelazhagar takes eṉai-t-tiṭpam to mean the other strengths listed under 661 (wealth, army, allies and the like), and ulaku (the world) to mean the wise or great, who alone set a proper value on things; Solomon Pappaiah follows this with uyarntōr (the eminent), while Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep ‘the world’ at large. The effect is to restate 661 as a judgement of worth: firmness in action outranks every other kind of strength. The three sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, do not yield to this degrading impotence. It does not become you. Give up such petty weakness of heart and arise, O chastiser of the enemy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna rebukes Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age, whose skill counts for nothing while he refuses to act.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna has every strength but, for a time, lacks resolve to act, which is exactly the person the Kural says the world will not value.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit: great ability undone by lack of resolve to act.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells a would-be follower that one who starts and then wavers is unfit for the work.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares the unsteady doer unwanted, whatever else he may offer.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on rejection of the wavering; spiritual rather than worldly context.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as though they are a [single] structure joined firmly.”
islam.explanation: Coming just after the rebuke of those who say what they do not do (61:2-3), the verse praises solid, unwavering action.
islam.tie_back: The positive side of the Kural: firmness in action is what is truly valued.
islam._accuracy_note: Values firmness in action; its setting is collective struggle rather than individual undertakings.

judaism.quote_or_event: “...one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it...”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says that wisdom without matching deeds is like a top-heavy tree, easily blown over.
judaism.tie_back: Wisdom without action, like the Kural’s ‘other strengths’ without firmness in action, cannot stand.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match: gifts unsupported by deeds are worthless.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says youth and strength are wasted on someone who will not exert himself when it is time to act.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Though young and strong’ is the Kural’s eṉai-t-tiṭpam: strengths that count for nothing without resolve to act.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on capacity wasted by lack of exertion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...you fight bravely, and no man with any justice can make light of your doings in battle. But you are careless and wilfully remiss. It grieves me to the heart to hear the ill that the Trojans speak about you...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector tells his brother Paris that his courage and skill are real, but his wilful slackness has made the Trojans despise him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Paris is the Kural’s case exactly: gifted, yet not esteemed, because he will not apply himself firmly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-direct match: acknowledged strengths cancelled by lack of firmness in action.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And as in the Olympic Games it is not the most beautiful and the strongest that are crowned but those who compete (for it is some of these that are victorious), so those who act win, and rightly win, the noble and good things in life.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtue as a mere capacity earns nothing; only those who act on it win the prize.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he denies honour to strength that does not act, however great.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match: capacity without action wins no crown.

ytamizh-ch67.title: Thirukkural Chapter 67: வினைத்திட்பம் / Power in Action (with Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar commentaries)

thirukkuralnet-adhigaram67.title: வினைத்திட்பம் - அதிகாரம் 67 (with Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi commentaries)
